title: Irregular verbs: possum, eo, fero, volo, fio

objectives.can: Recognise and parse the common forms of possum, eo, fero, volo, nolo and fio, and their compounds.

explanation.summary: A handful of very common Latin verbs do not follow the four conjugations in the present system. They are short, old and frequent, so you meet them in nearly every verse: 'can', 'go', 'bring', 'wish', 'not wish', 'prefer' and 'become'. This lesson shows what is irregular in each, and how their compounds behave.

sections.heading: possum: 'I am able'
body: *possum* is a compound of an old adjective meaning 'able' and the verb *sum*, so it is conjugated like *sum* with the front part pot- before a vowel and pos- before an s. In the present: *possum*, *potes*, *potest*, *possumus*, *potestis*, *possunt*. The imperfect is *poteram* and the future *potero*, formed like those of *sum* (*eram*, *ero*) with pot- in front.

The verb usually takes an infinitive to complete its sense: in John 7:34, *non potestis venire* is 'you cannot come'. It means 'can' or 'am able to', and the English 'can' has no matching forms for the other tenses, so translate the imperfect 'was able' and the future 'will be able'.

sections.heading: eo: 'I go'
body: *eo* has the stem e- before a, o and u, and i- elsewhere: e-o, i-s, i-t, i-mus, i-tis, e-unt. The imperfect adds -ba- to i-: *ibat*, *ibant*. The future adds -bo-: *ibimus* in John 6:69, 'we shall go'. In both tenses the verb follows the pattern of the first and second conjugations (compare *laudabit*), not the third.

Its many compounds go the same way. In this course they are separate headwords: *exeo* 'go out' (*exeunt*, *exibat*), *transeo* 'go across' (*transit*, *transibit*), *redeo* 'go back' (*redit*), *abeo* 'go away' and *ineo* 'go in'. They are the commonest verbs of movement in the Gospels. Note that the form *eo* is ambiguous: it is also the ablative of the pronoun *is*.

sections.heading: fero: 'I carry, bring, bear'
body: *fero* is a third-conjugation verb that drops the connecting vowel in the singular and in the second person plural: fer-o, fer-s, fer-t, fer-imus, fer-tis, fer-unt. So *fert* in John 15:5 is 'he bears' (of the branch that bears fruit). The imperfect is regular (*ferebat*, *ferebant*).

Its compounds are formed with prefixes whose last letter often changes to match the f: *offero* (ob- + fero), *affero* (ad- + fero), *aufero* (ab- + fero) and *refero*. Their present follows *fero* (*offers*, *offert*, *offertis*, *aufert*). The perfect of all of them comes from a different stem (compare *tulerunt* and *obtulerunt*), which is taught with the principal parts.

sections.heading: volo, nolo, malo: wishing and preferring
body: *volo* means 'I wish, I am willing'; *nolo* is its negative (from *ne* and *volo*) and *malo* is 'I prefer' (from *magis* and *volo*). Like *volo*, they take an infinitive: *non vultis venire* in John 5:40 is 'you are not willing to come'. The singular and the second plural of *volo* are irregular: vol-o, vi-s, vul-t, vol-umus, vul-tis, vol-unt. *nolo* follows it with the negative in front (nol-o, non vi-s, non vul-t, nol-umus, non vul-tis, nol-unt), and *malo* with ma- (mal-o, ma-vi-s, ma-vul-t, mal-umus, ma-vul-tis, mal-unt).

The imperfects are regular: *volebat*, *nolebat*, *malebam*. Some of the editions print u for v (*uolebat*). One short answer in Matthew 21:29, *Nolo*, shows how forceful a single word can be: 'I will not'. The analysis files a few forms of a different verb, *volo*, *volare* 'fly', under the same headword; the exercises in this lesson avoid them.

sections.heading: fio: 'I become, I am made'
body: *fio* is active in form but passive in sense: it serves as the passive of *facio* in the present system. *facit* is 'he makes'; *fit* is 'it is made' or 'it becomes' or 'it happens'. The forms in the texts are *fit*, *fiunt*, *fiebat*, *fiet*, *fient*; the other persons are rare. The infinitive is *fieri*.

The forms of the perfect passive of *facio* are formed with a participle and *sum* (taught later). The analyser tags *fio* as active, since its endings are active; this is a feature of the verb, not a mistake in the tag. In John 15:7, *fiet vobis* is 'it will be done for you'.

misunderstandings: The pot- of *possum* is not a prefix that goes away: it changes to pos- only before an s (possum, possumus, possunt, but potest, potestis, poteram).
*eo* is not always the verb 'I go': it is also the ablative of *is* ('by him', 'in it'). The verb has the first person singular ending -o; the pronoun is read from the sentence.
*fit* does not mean 'he makes'. It is the passive or intransitive counterpart of *facit*: 'it is made', 'it becomes', 'it happens'.

*nolo* is not a separate verb with its own forms: it is *volo* with the negative before it (non vi-s, non vul-t), and *malo* is *volo* with ma- before it. Do not confuse *malo*, 'I prefer', with the adjective *malus*, 'bad'.

deeper.heading: Why the commonest verbs are irregular
body: Verbs that are used constantly tend to keep old forms, short forms and forms that mix stems. The same thing happens in English with 'go' and 'went', or 'am', 'was' and 'be'. That is the usual explanation of the Latin irregular verbs, and it is why their forms must simply be learned, as they cannot be derived from a rule.

examples.analysis: Two irregular verbs in one sentence. *fert* is the third person singular of *fero*: 'he bears (fruit)'. It is a bare fer- + t, with no vowel between. *potestis* is the second person plural of *possum*: 'you are able'. With *facere* after it, *potestis facere* means 'you can do'. The pot- shows because the next letter is e.

examples.analysis: *ibimus* is the first person plural of the future of *eo*: 'we shall go'. The stem is i-, the future sign is -bi- and the ending is -mus. Peter's question *ad quem ibimus?* uses the same tense sign as *videbimus* or *laudabimus*.

examples.analysis: *vultis* is the second person plural of the present of *volo*: 'you wish'. Where the regular verb would have vol-itis, the irregular form has vul-tis. It is followed by the infinitive *venire* ('to come') to complete its sense, and negated by *non*.

examples.analysis: *Nolo* is the first person singular of the present of *nolo*: 'I am unwilling', 'I will not'. It stands alone as the whole answer, as a verb can in Latin, with its subject in the ending.

examples.analysis: *fiet* is the third person singular of the future of *fio*: 'it will become' or 'it will be done'. The tense sign is -e- after the stem fi-, as in the third conjugation, and there is no b. The passive sense is the point: it is what happens to the things you ask for.

check.prompt: aufert and auferebat are two forms of aufero (carry off, take away). In what do they differ?
check.explain: aufert is present; auferebat is imperfect. In person and number they agree.

check.prompt: nolunt and nolebant are two forms of nolo. In what do they differ?
check.explain: nolunt is present; nolebant is imperfect. In person and number they agree.

check.prompt: abibunt and abibant are two forms of abeo (go away, depart). In what do they differ?
check.explain: abibunt is future; abibant is imperfect. In person and number they agree.

check.prompt: referebam and refero are two forms of refero (carry back, report). In what do they differ?
check.explain: referebam is imperfect; refero is present. In person and number they agree.

check.prompt: ibunt and eunt are two forms of eo (to go). In what do they differ?
check.explain: ibunt is future; eunt is present. In person and number they agree.

check.prompt: *potestis* is marked. Why does it have pot- and not pos-?

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: I am the vine: you the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit: for without me you can do nothing.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: Because pot- stands before an e, and pos- only before an s
Because the verb is a compound of fero
check.explain: possum is pot- + sum. The t is kept before the e of es, est, estis; before an s it is assimilated (possum, possumus, possunt).

check.prompt: *fiet* is marked. What does the verse do with *fio*?

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, you shall ask whatever you will, and it shall be done unto you.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: It is the present of fio: 'it is done'
It is the active future of facio: 'he will make'
It is the future of fero: 'he will bring'
It is the future of fio, which is passive in sense: 'it will be done'
check.explain: fio serves as the passive of facio. fiet, the future, means 'it will be done' or 'it will become'. The active future of facio would be faciet.

reading.why: Four verses of the vine and the branches: fert, potestis, fiet (and the compound forms around them) in one passage, with the irregular verbs of the lesson doing real work.
